facts.label: Version, perimeter and duplicate relationships
facts.text: - Reporting entity changed inside the series. The 10-K and Q1 10-Q are joint reports and statements of Carnival Corporation & plc. The Q2 10-Q states: "In May 2026, we completed the unification of the dual listed company structure under a single company, Carnival Corporation Ltd." (Q2 10-Q page:5). The Q3 10-Q repeats this and states the migration of legal incorporation from Panama to Bermuda (Q3 10-Q page:5). Every period comparison that crosses February 28, 2026 and May 31, 2026 crosses this boundary. The Q3 10-Q equity statement shows the line "DLC unification share exchange and related costs" (Q3 10-Q page:4). The Q3 10-Q states "There have been no material changes to our business, including strategy, underlying assets and operations" (Q3 10-Q page:5); this is a management statement in a filed document and is not a fidelity review of the series. - Release entity names move with the filings: the Q1 release is headed "CARNIVAL CORPORATION & PLC" and the Q2 and Q3 releases "CARNIVAL CORPORATION LTD." in their statements. - No source is a duplicate of another. The three 10-Qs and three releases are distinct periods; the Q3 release statements repeat the Q3 10-Q statements and are not an independent source for the same figures. The 10-K is the retained source for fiscal 2025 figures; the Q3 10-Q repeats the November 30, 2025 balance sheet as a comparative, with presentation changes noted below. - Issuer, borrower, guarantor roles: the context names no borrower, parent or guarantors. The Q3 10-Q debt table groups debt as "Unsecured Subsidiary Guaranteed" and "Unsecured (No Subsidiary Guarantee)" and states "all of our outstanding debt is issued or guaranteed by substantially the same entities with the exception of the $1.7 billion of export credit facilities of Sun Princess Limited and Sun Princess II Limited" (Q3 10-Q page:10). Individual issuers and guarantor lists per instrument are not in the pack; the entity-by-instrument mapping is an open distinction (see Gaps).

facts.label: Financial base view
facts.text: Carnival's financial base at August 31, 2026 is a large, cash-generative cruise operator whose reported leverage is improving through deliberate debt repayment, with earnings broadly flat at the operating line and a growing claim on cash from ship commitments and shareholder returns. Evidence: revenue was 8,435 in the quarter against 8,153 a year earlier and 21,263 for nine months against 20,292, while operating income was 2,220 against 2,271 in the quarter and 3,678 against 3,748 for nine months (Q3 10-Q page:2). Fuel expense rose to 615 from 451 in the quarter (Q3 10-Q page:2), and the MD&A attributes 149 of the operating expense increase to higher fuel prices (Q3 10-Q page:22). Mechanism: pricing and onboard spend are growing faster than capacity, but fuel and other costs absorb the gain at the operating line, so the credit improvement comes from the financing side. Net income rose to 2,725 for nine months from 2,348, helped by interest expense net of capitalized interest falling to 862 from 1,034 and debt extinguishment costs falling to 23 from 366 (Q3 10-Q page:2).

facts.label: Financial base view
facts.text: On the metrics built here, EBITDA (operating income plus depreciation and amortization, unadjusted) for the twelve months to August 31, 2026 is 7,311 against 7,273 for fiscal 2025, an increase of 38, while principal debt fell by 2,824 to 24,559 (Q3 10-Q page:9). Total debt to EBITDA therefore moved from 3.77 to 3.36 and net debt to EBITDA from 3.50 to 3.19. The improvement is a debt-reduction effect, not an earnings effect. Between May 31, 2026 and August 31, 2026 the net debt figure rose by 12 to 23,339, because the 1,011 reduction in principal debt was funded from cash, which fell by 1,023 to 1,220, while the company also paid dividends of 204 and repurchased shares worth 549 in the quarter (Q3 10-Q page:2, page:4, page:9). Creditor read: the next leg of deleveraging depends on EBITDA growth and on how much of operating cash flow is directed to shareholders, since management targets distribution of more than 40 percent of cash from operations (approximately $14 billion through 2029) and a 2.75x net debt to adjusted EBITDA ratio (Q1 release page:3, page:4), against a company-reported 3.1x at May 31, 2026 (Q2 release page:3).

facts.label: Business and transaction view
facts.text: Carnival Corporation Ltd. is a Bermuda-incorporated, NYSE-listed cruise operator with eight brands, 94 ships and 272,380 lower-berth capacity at November 30, 2025, a tour business in Alaska and the Yukon, and seven owned or operated ports and destinations, which together form a cruise and destination business sold through travel agents and company websites (10-K page:10, page:12, page:15; Q3 10-Q page:1). Evidence: ticket revenue of 13,825 and onboard and other revenue of 7,438 for the nine months to August 31, 2026 (Q3 10-Q page:2), and customer deposits of 7,639 (Q3 release page:9). Mechanism: guests pay deposits months in advance and the balance before sailing, so deposits are collected before cost is incurred and form a large current liability, which the company describes as the reason for a structural working capital deficit (Q3 10-Q page:25). The third quarter carries the largest share of operating income (2,220 of the nine-month 3,678, or 60.4 percent), so earnings are seasonal and credit-relevant events in the northern summer weigh disproportionately. Creditor read: revenue visibility is high because of advance bookings (management states 2027 booked occupancy and pricing at record levels, Q3 release page:1, management language), margin resilience depends on fuel and commissions, and cash conversion is supported by deposits, but a fleet-wide shock is uninsured for loss of earnings (10-K page:19).

facts.label: Business and transaction view
facts.text: The transaction history that matters is structural. The dual listed company of Carnival Corporation (Panama) and Carnival plc (England and Wales), operated as a single economic enterprise with identical boards but separate legal identities (10-K page:7), was unified in May 2026 under Carnival Corporation Ltd. (Bermuda), listed solely on the NYSE, with Carnival plc shares exchanged one-for-one (Q3 10-Q page:5). The group states there were no material changes to its business after the unification (Q3 10-Q page:5, management language). Over fiscal 2025 the company refinanced heavily: it issued six series of senior unsecured notes, took 1.0 billion of unsecured term loans and a 4.5 billion revolving facility, and prepaid 11.6 billion of debt including all secured term loans, with 409 of extinguishment and modification costs (10-K page:80, page:81, page:63). In the nine months to August 31, 2026 it issued no debt, settled the 1.1 billion convertible notes in shares and cash of 500, and redeemed the 7.00% notes due 2029 (500) with cash on hand (Q3 10-Q page:3, page:10; Q3 release page:3). The effect is a simpler, fully unsecured debt stack with lower interest cost, but one in which several subsidiary guarantees were also released (Q3 10-Q page:10). No sponsor is identified, no controlling holder is disclosed and no dividend recapitalisation is documented in the supplied sources. Distributions resumed with a dividend declared in December 2025 and a 2.5 billion buyback authorized in March 2026, funded in the nine months from operating cash flow rather than new debt (10-K page:62; Q1 release page:4; Q3 10-Q page:3, page:28). Behaviour read at issuer level: Supportive on deleveraging and reporting transparency, Neutral or Mixed on capital allocation because debt is being repaid while distributions rise, and unresolved on the release of security and guarantees because the documents that permit and govern it are not supplied.

facts.label: Transaction summary and new debt issues
facts.text: Unification and redomiciliation (status: completed May 2026). The boards of Carnival Corporation and Carnival plc recommended unifying the dual listed company under Carnival Corporation as the single listed parent, with Carnival plc shareholders receiving shares on a one-for-one basis and a move of incorporation from Panama to Bermuda; the plan was described as expected to preserve shareholder voting and economic rights (10-K page:7, management language). It was subject to shareholder, regulatory and UK court approvals and shareholder meetings in April 2026 (10-K page:8). The Q2 10-Q states it was completed in May 2026 (Q2 10-Q page:5) and the exhibit list of the Q3 10-Q includes a termination agreement dated May 6, 2026 between the corporation and Carnival plc and the memorandum and bye-laws of Carnival Corporation Ltd. (Q3 10-Q page:28). Uses of proceeds and debt raised: none, it is a share exchange with related costs shown in equity (Q3 10-Q page:4). Liquidity effect: not stated in the sources. Creditor mechanics: debt that was previously issued or guaranteed by "substantially the same entities" remains so (Q3 10-Q page:10), the obligor perimeter for a planned shelf is Carnival Corporation Ltd. with Carnival UK Ltd. (Q3 10-Q page:26), and the treatment of the former Carnival plc debt guarantees is not described. The sources do not give debt-document terms, so legal capacity for any future priming or release is Insufficient Information.

facts.label: Transaction summary and new debt issues
facts.text: New debt issues, fiscal 2025 (status: completed). Senior unsecured notes: 1.3 billion 5.13% due 2029, 1.0 billion 5.75% due 2030, 1.0 billion 5.88% due 2031, 1.2 billion 4.13% euro notes due 2031, 3.0 billion 5.75% due 2032 and 2.0 billion 6.13% due 2033; unsecured term loans maturing in 2027 of 0.4 billion, 0.3 billion and 0.3 billion at SOFR plus 1.13%, 1.25% and 1.38%; a 4.5 billion unsecured multi-currency revolving credit facility maturing June 2030 with a 1.0 billion accordion; 0.8 billion of export credit borrowings (10-K page:80, page:81). Use of proceeds: with cash on hand, they prepaid 7.63% notes due 2026, 5.75% notes due 2027, first-priority secured term loans due 2027 and 2028, 10.38% senior priority notes due 2028, 6.00% notes due 2029 and 10.50% notes due 2030, an aggregate 11.6 billion, with 409 of debt extinguishment and modification costs including 271 premium paid (10-K page:81). Liquidity effect: 6.4 billion of liquidity at November 30, 2025 with 4.5 billion revolver availability (10-K page:59). Maturity effect: the new notes mature in 2029 to 2033 (10-K page:79).

facts.label: Transaction summary and new debt issues
facts.text: Fiscal 2026 to August 31, 2026 (status: completed unless stated). No new debt issued (Q3 10-Q page:3). The 1.1 billion 5.75% convertible notes were settled in December 2025: 69.1 million shares issued and 500 cash (Q3 10-Q page:10). The 7.00% notes due 2029 (500) became unsecured in June 2026 and were then redeemed with cash on hand, with 23 of extinguishment costs (Q3 10-Q page:10; Q3 release page:3). The 7.88% notes due 2027 and 4.00% notes due 2028 are no longer secured, and the company states it has no remaining secured debt (Q3 10-Q page:10; Q3 release page:3, management language). Several unsecured notes, loans and export credit facilities are no longer subject to subsidiary guarantees (Q3 10-Q page:10). Rating events: a Moody's upgrade with a positive outlook (Q2 release page:3) and an S&P upgrade giving a second investment grade rating (Q3 release page:3); levels are not supplied. Planned: a Form S-3 expected on September 29, 2026 for debt securities guaranteed by Carnival UK Ltd. (Q3 10-Q page:26, status: expected, not confirmed as filed). Total debt moved from 27,383 to 24,559 and liquidity from 6,428 to 5,720 (CP-1). Shareholder-return actions: dividend reinstated in December 2025 at 0.15 per share quarterly; initial 2.5 billion buyback announced in March 2026 without expiry; dividends of 618 and repurchases of 929 in the nine months (10-K page:62; Q1 release page:4; Q3 10-Q page:3).

facts.label: Credit translations
facts.text: - Revenue durability. Evidence: advance bookings and customer deposits of 7,639 (Q3 release page:9) with record 2027 booked occupancy and pricing stated by management (Q3 release page:1). Mechanic: deposits and balance payments arrive before voyage cost, so cash converts early and revenue is visible several months ahead; most revenue is ticket (65.0 percent) and sourced largely from United States guests (55.8 percent of nine-month revenue, Q3 10-Q page:8). Implication: revenue is durable in ordinary conditions, but a sourcing-market or geopolitical shock lands on a concentrated base and on a peak quarter that earns 60.4 percent of nine-month operating income; the Q2 release cites disruption in the Mediterranean from the Middle East conflict (Q2 release page:2). Countering conflict: none logged. - Margin and cash-flow risk. Evidence: fuel 615 against 451 in the quarter and operating income down despite revenue growth (Q3 10-Q page:2). Mechanic: fuel cost per metric ton rose to 826 from 607 and is partly offset by lower fuel consumption per thousand ALBDs (26.9 against 28.0, Q3 10-Q page:21). Implication: earnings are exposed to fuel; the sensitivity of 59 per 10 percent move in fuel price for the fourth quarter is a management figure (Q3 release page:5). - Concentration and structure. Evidence: obligor group revenue of 9,636 against consolidated 21,263 for nine months (Q3 10-Q page:26, page:2). Mechanic: guaranteed shelf debt would be backed by a group earning under half of consolidated revenue. Implication: ranking depends on guarantor coverage that the documents must confirm. - Sponsor alignment and control. Evidence: no sponsor or controlling holder identified; distributions funded from operations (above). Mechanic: shareholder-return policy is set by management and boards. Implication: alignment is with public shareholders; creditor protection rests on covenants and rating-linked pricing, not on an owner's support. - Key uncertainties: legal terms (indentures, guarantee release triggers), covenant headroom, the cause of the guarantee releases and rating levels.

rows.label: Carnival is a diversified, seasonal cruise operator with eight brands whose main transaction in the period was the May 2026 unification into one Bermuda company, alongside deleveraging, secured debt release and rising shareholder returns.
Revenue is 65.0 percent ticket and 35.0 percent onboard, sold mostly through advance bookings, and the third quarter earns most of the operating income.
The two listed companies became one Bermuda company in May 2026, and the group says operations did not change.
Security was released and several subsidiary guarantees were released while ratings rose, and no new debt was issued in nine months.
Management targets distributing more than 40 percent of cash from operations through 2029 and net leverage of 2.75x, with a 2.5 billion buyback.
The company states it carries no loss-of-earnings or revenue insurance.

facts.label: Credit view
facts.text: Carnival Corporation Ltd. has a strong and improving fundamental credit profile, but its improvement so far comes from repaying debt rather than from earnings growth. Its strongest support is visible, deposit-funded demand (customer deposits of USD 7,639 million) and liquidity of USD 5,720 million with debt that is now unsecured and falling, to USD 24,559 million at August 31, 2026. The weakest point is that LTM EBITDA of USD 7,311 million is almost unchanged from USD 7,273 million for fiscal 2025, while fuel costs rise, loss of earnings is uninsured, and shareholder returns and USD 18.3 billion of ship commitments compete for cash. What decides the outcome is whether EBITDA grows enough to keep net debt to EBITDA, now 3.19x, falling while distributions rise.

facts.label: Key findings
facts.text: First, leverage fell because debt fell, not because earnings grew. Total debt (principal) fell from USD 27,383 million at November 30, 2025 to USD 24,559 million at August 31, 2026, while LTM EBITDA (operating income plus depreciation and amortization, unadjusted) rose only from USD 7,273 million to USD 7,311 million; total debt to EBITDA moved from 3.77x to 3.36x and net debt to EBITDA from 3.50x to 3.19x [CP-1, Chart data: leverage]. Because the repayment was funded from cash, net debt rose by USD 12 million over the third quarter, from USD 23,327 million to USD 23,339 million, while the company paid dividends of USD 204 million and repurchased shares worth USD 549 million in the quarter [CP-1, Financial base view]. For creditors this means the next step down in leverage requires either further repayment, which competes with distributions, or EBITDA growth.

facts.label: Key findings
facts.text: Second, near-term liquidity is sound but maturities depend on refinancing or cash flow. Liquidity is USD 5,720 million (cash USD 1,220 million plus USD 4,500 million available under a revolving facility maturing in June 2030) against current debt of USD 2,036 million, and no letters of credit usage is printed [CP-1, Chart data: liquidity]. Scheduled principal is USD 301 million for the remainder of 2026, USD 2,517 million in 2027, USD 3,961 million in 2028, USD 3,631 million in 2029 and USD 2,885 million in 2030 [CP-1, Chart data: debt maturities], which total USD 13,295 million through 2030 against LTM cash from operations less capital expenditure of USD 3,176 million. Management states the company has two investment grade ratings, and the revolver pricing is linked to ratings, but rating levels are not supplied [CP-1A, Transaction summary and new debt issues]. The implication is that debt service is comfortable but principal reduction at the recent pace relies on cash flow, and a larger part relies on market access.

facts.label: Key findings
facts.text: Third, operating earnings are flat while costs rise, which limits cushion. In the third quarter revenue was USD 8,435 million against USD 8,153 million, while operating income was USD 2,220 million against USD 2,271 million, as fuel expense rose to USD 615 million from USD 451 million [CP-1, Financial base view]. Net income benefited from lower interest (USD 285 million in the quarter against USD 317 million) and lower debt extinguishment costs. Accrual EBITDA to interest expense is 6.21x on an LTM basis, but cash interest cover exists only for fiscal 2025 at 6.06x [CP-1, Chart data: interest cover]. Management guides fiscal 2026 adjusted EBITDA to approximately USD 7.14 billion, a management forecast rather than a result [CP-1, Latest quarter and after]. Fuel exposure is therefore the main near-term earnings swing factor for debt service.

The company states it carries no insurance for loss of earnings or revenue [CP-1A, Company and operating model]. After the May 2026 unification into one Bermuda parent, all debt is unsecured, the 7.00% notes were redeemed, and notes, loans and export credit facilities of about USD 12,520 million on the recast basis moved to the no-subsidiary-guarantee category [CP-1, Debt schedule; CP-1A, Transaction summary and new debt issues]. The obligor group planned for a guaranteed shelf earned 45.3 percent of consolidated nine-month revenue [CP-1, Perimeter and reporting basis]. facts.text: Sixth, capital allocation is the main discretionary variable. Dividends of USD 618 million and repurchases of USD 929 million in nine months equal 48.9 percent of cash from operations less capital expenditure; management targets distributing more than 40 percent of cash from operations by 2029 and a net debt to adjusted EBITDA ratio of 2.75x, and ship commitments have risen to USD 18.3 billion against USD 10.7 billion of undrawn export credit [CP-1, Cash flow and capital returns; CP-1A, Capital allocation and governance behaviour]. For comparison, reaching 2.75x on the unadjusted metric used here would need net debt lower by USD 3,234 million at constant EBITDA, or EBITDA of USD 8,487 million at constant net debt (see Calculations); the management target is defined on adjusted EBITDA and a minimum cash balance, so this is an illustration of scale only. Creditors depend on management choosing deleveraging over faster distributions, and the documents that could constrain that choice are not supplied.

facts.label: Strengths and weaknesses
facts.text: Strengths. The business has high demand visibility: customer deposits of USD 7,639 million, record 2027 booked occupancy and pricing as stated by management, and 93 percent of 2026 booked at the time of the second quarter release [CP-1A, Company and operating model], so revenue and cash arrive ahead of voyage cost. The group is diversified across eight brands and two segments, with 94 ships and 272,380 lower-berth capacity, so a problem at one brand does not stop the group [CP-1A, Company profile]. Debt is falling, now unsecured, and mostly fixed-rate (52 percent fixed plus 33 percent euro fixed), with euro debt (43 percent including floating) matched against euro-functional operations, which limits rate and currency sensitivity [CP-1, Debt schedule]. Liquidity of USD 5,720 million exceeds current debt of USD 2,036 million, and USD 10.7 billion of undrawn export credit pre-funds part of the ship commitments [CP-1, Liquidity].

The cutoff in the context is 2026-11-05, the current period is q3-2026 (quarter ended 2026-08-31), the prior period is fy-2025 (fiscal year ended 2025-11-30) and the reporting currency is USD. The question is whether the supplied source set can support the requested downstream work (CP-1, CP-1A, CP-2, CP-5) and what remains blocked. This module gives no credit conclusion, legal interpretation or investment opinion, and it does not normalize or reconcile figures. The context file lists no deal terms, quotes, ratings, peers, assumptions or research questions, and states `legal_documents` as `none`; it is not issuer evidence.

### Reader summary

### Readiness view

The effective source set is READY_WITH_LIMITATIONS for each requested consumer (CP-1, CP-1A, CP-2 and CP-5). All 7 issuer sources are filed or furnished documents with extracted text on every page (246 of 246 pages carry text, 0 blank). The filed 10-K and 10-Qs hold the authority for statements, debt, covenants, commitments and legal matters; the earnings releases are furnished management documents and supply non-GAAP reconciliations, guidance and attributed narrative only. Nothing is blocked and no consumer is conditional: no critical identity boundary is unresolved, although the reporting entity changed in May 2026. The main restrictions are a perimeter change inside the series (a combined two-registrant group through the first quarter 2026, a single Bermuda registrant afterwards), the absence of fiscal 2025 adjusted EBITDA and of interim cash interest paid, the absence of any legal financing document or rating report, and possible release graphics that text extraction does not show. Source sufficiency here does not mean any downstream analysis is complete, and no extraction fidelity review has been done. The next evidence action is to obtain the fourth quarter 2025 earnings release or another source for fiscal 2025 adjusted EBITDA, and the debt documents, before leverage, coverage and ranking conclusions are drawn.

## Findings
### Reader summary
| Bottom line | Confidence | Main limitation |

| Leverage fell because debt was repaid, not because earnings grew: total debt to EBITDA 3.36 and net debt to EBITDA 3.19 at August 31, 2026, against 3.77 and 3.50 at fiscal 2025. | Medium | EBITDA is operating income plus depreciation and amortization; fiscal 2025 adjusted EBITDA and interim cash interest are not supplied. |
| Finding | Creditor impact | Confidence |

| Revenue grew while operating income slipped, as fuel cost rose; net income rose on lower interest and lower debt extinguishment costs. | Earnings quality depends on fuel and on interest savings that come from repaying debt. | High |

| Net debt was almost unchanged between May 31, 2026 and August 31, 2026, because cash paid for debt repayment and shareholder returns. | Further net leverage gains now rely on earnings growth, as cash is being returned to shareholders. | Medium |

| All debt is now unsecured, and 2,036 of debt is current against cash of 1,220. | Current debt exceeds cash but is covered by liquidity of 5,720; later maturities rely on cash flow or refinancing. | Medium |

| Ship purchase commitments are 18.3 billion, against 10.7 billion of undrawn export credit. | Newbuild spending is partly pre-financed; the rest is a call on cash flow after shareholder returns. | Medium |
| Covenant compliance is stated, but covenant ratios are not printed and the proxies do not match the contract definitions. | Headroom cannot be measured from the filings. | High |
### Financial base view

Carnival's financial base at August 31, 2026 is a large, cash-generative cruise operator whose reported leverage is improving through deliberate debt repayment, with earnings broadly flat at the operating line and a growing claim on cash from ship commitments and shareholder returns. Evidence: revenue was 8,435 in the quarter against 8,153 a year earlier and 21,263 for nine months against 20,292, while operating income was 2,220 against 2,271 in the quarter and 3,678 against 3,748 for nine months (Q3 10-Q page:2). Fuel expense rose to 615 from 451 in the quarter (Q3 10-Q page:2), and the MD&A attributes 149 of the operating expense increase to higher fuel prices (Q3 10-Q page:22). Mechanism: pricing and onboard spend are growing faster than capacity, but fuel and other costs absorb the gain at the operating line, so the credit improvement comes from the financing side. Net income rose to 2,725 for nine months from 2,348, helped by interest expense net of capitalized interest falling to 862 from 1,034 and debt extinguishment costs falling to 23 from 366 (Q3 10-Q page:2).

On the metrics built here, EBITDA (operating income plus depreciation and amortization, unadjusted) for the twelve months to August 31, 2026 is 7,311 against 7,273 for fiscal 2025, an increase of 38, while principal debt fell by 2,824 to 24,559 (Q3 10-Q page:9). Total debt to EBITDA therefore moved from 3.77 to 3.36 and net debt to EBITDA from 3.50 to 3.19. The improvement is a debt-reduction effect, not an earnings effect. Between May 31, 2026 and August 31, 2026 the net debt figure rose by 12 to 23,339, because the 1,011 reduction in principal debt was funded from cash, which fell by 1,023 to 1,220, while the company also paid dividends of 204 and repurchased shares worth 549 in the quarter (Q3 10-Q page:2, page:4, page:9). Creditor read: the next leg of deleveraging depends on EBITDA growth and on how much of operating cash flow is directed to shareholders, since management targets distribution of more than 40 percent of cash from operations (approximately $14 billion through 2029) and a 2.75x net debt to adjusted EBITDA ratio (Q1 release page:3, page:4), against a company-reported 3.1x at May 31, 2026 (Q2 release page:3).

Structure and liquidity: all remaining debt is unsecured after the 7.00% notes due 2029 were redeemed and the 7.88% 2027 and 4.00% 2028 notes were released from security (Q3 10-Q page:10; Q3 release page:3), which improves flexibility but leaves the 20.6 billion net book value of ships under negative pledges (Q3 10-Q page:10). Liquidity is 5,720 (cash 1,220 plus 4,500 available under the revolving facility, which runs to June 2030), against a stated minimum liquidity covenant of 1,500 (Q3 10-Q page:10, page:25). Undrawn export credit facilities of 10.7 billion fund ship deliveries and are not general liquidity. Ship commitments rose to 18.3 billion from 11.9 billion at November 30, 2025, almost entirely in the "thereafter" bucket (11.4 billion), consistent with the three Princess LNG ship orders announced for delivery in 2035, 2038 and 2039 (Q2 release page:4); the link between the order and the increase is an inference, since the 10-Q does not itemize the order.

Limitations that restrict conclusions: fiscal 2025 adjusted EBITDA is not supplied, so every leverage and coverage figure uses unadjusted operating income plus depreciation and amortization and is not the company's measure; interim cash paid for interest is not printed; covenant ratios are not printed; issuer and guarantor by instrument are not printed. Confidence is Medium overall: reported statements are High, derived leverage and coverage are Medium.

### Perimeter and reporting basis

- Reporting entity. The 10-K and the first quarter report are joint reports of Carnival Corporation and Carnival plc with statements titled "CARNIVAL CORPORATION & PLC" (10-K page:63; Q1 10-Q page:2). The second and third quarter reports are those of Carnival Corporation Ltd. after the unification completed in May 2026 (Q2 10-Q page:5; Q3 10-Q page:5). The consolidated group is the same: the Q3 10-Q states "There have been no material changes to our business, including strategy, underlying assets and operations" (Q3 10-Q page:5). Amounts for fiscal 2025 and the nine months of 2025 are therefore used as the same group, a judgment based on that statement and on the equity statement showing the share exchange (Q3 10-Q page:4).

- Obligor perimeter. The Q3 10-Q gives summarized information for the obligor group of Carnival Corporation Ltd. and Carnival UK Ltd. for a planned guaranteed debt shelf (Q3 10-Q page:26): revenues of 9,636 for nine months to August 31, 2026 against consolidated revenues of 21,263, and 12,910 for the year to November 30, 2025 against 26,622 (10-K page:63). The obligor group therefore earned under half of consolidated revenue (45.3 percent of nine-month revenue, 48.5 percent of fiscal 2025) and 1,604 of nine-month operating income against 3,678 consolidated. At August 31, 2026 it was owed 3,093 by non-obligor subsidiaries and had noncurrent liabilities of 22,022. This suggests that creditors of the parent-level notes rely in part on intercompany balances and subsidiary guarantees (an inference); the guarantor list per instrument is not supplied.

- Reclassification. Fiscal 2025 comparatives in the Q3 10-Q separate noncontrolling interests of 14 from additional paid-in capital (17,253 against 17,267 in the 10-K); total equity is 12,284 in both (10-K page:64; Q3 10-Q page:3, page:5). Net income used here is the total before noncontrolling interests (1,923 for the quarter) unless stated.

## Findings
### Reader summary
| Bottom line | Confidence | Main limitation |

| Carnival is a diversified, seasonal cruise operator with eight brands whose main transaction in the period was the May 2026 unification into one Bermuda company, alongside deleveraging, secured debt release and rising shareholder returns. | Medium | Indentures, guarantor lists, ownership percentages and rating levels are not supplied, so legal creditor position is not assessable. |
| Finding | Creditor impact | Confidence |

| Revenue is 65.0 percent ticket and 35.0 percent onboard, sold mostly through advance bookings, and the third quarter earns most of the operating income. | Customer deposits fund operations and make cash flow seasonal; a demand shock hits the peak quarter hardest. | High |

| The two listed companies became one Bermuda company in May 2026, and the group says operations did not change. | Debt now sits under one parent with a guarantee structure that has changed; legal ranking needs the debt documents. | Medium |

| Security was released and several subsidiary guarantees were released while ratings rose, and no new debt was issued in nine months. | Holders of previously secured notes have less structural protection; the cause and indenture terms are not shown. | Medium |

| Management targets distributing more than 40 percent of cash from operations through 2029 and net leverage of 2.75x, with a 2.5 billion buyback. | Distribution capacity competes with deleveraging, with discretion resting with management. | Medium |
| The company states it carries no loss-of-earnings or revenue insurance. | A fleet-wide disruption would fall on cash flow and liquidity without insurance offset. | High |
### Business and transaction view

Carnival Corporation Ltd. is a Bermuda-incorporated, NYSE-listed cruise operator with eight brands, 94 ships and 272,380 lower-berth capacity at November 30, 2025, a tour business in Alaska and the Yukon, and seven owned or operated ports and destinations, which together form a cruise and destination business sold through travel agents and company websites (10-K page:10, page:12, page:15; Q3 10-Q page:1). Evidence: ticket revenue of 13,825 and onboard and other revenue of 7,438 for the nine months to August 31, 2026 (Q3 10-Q page:2), and customer deposits of 7,639 (Q3 release page:9). Mechanism: guests pay deposits months in advance and the balance before sailing, so deposits are collected before cost is incurred and form a large current liability, which the company describes as the reason for a structural working capital deficit (Q3 10-Q page:25). The third quarter carries the largest share of operating income (2,220 of the nine-month 3,678, or 60.4 percent), so earnings are seasonal and credit-relevant events in the northern summer weigh disproportionately. Creditor read: revenue visibility is high because of advance bookings (management states 2027 booked occupancy and pricing at record levels, Q3 release page:1, management language), margin resilience depends on fuel and commissions, and cash conversion is supported by deposits, but a fleet-wide shock is uninsured for loss of earnings (10-K page:19).

The transaction history that matters is structural. The dual listed company of Carnival Corporation (Panama) and Carnival plc (England and Wales), operated as a single economic enterprise with identical boards but separate legal identities (10-K page:7), was unified in May 2026 under Carnival Corporation Ltd. (Bermuda), listed solely on the NYSE, with Carnival plc shares exchanged one-for-one (Q3 10-Q page:5). The group states there were no material changes to its business after the unification (Q3 10-Q page:5, management language). Over fiscal 2025 the company refinanced heavily: it issued six series of senior unsecured notes, took 1.0 billion of unsecured term loans and a 4.5 billion revolving facility, and prepaid 11.6 billion of debt including all secured term loans, with 409 of extinguishment and modification costs (10-K page:80, page:81, page:63). In the nine months to August 31, 2026 it issued no debt, settled the 1.1 billion convertible notes in shares and cash of 500, and redeemed the 7.00% notes due 2029 (500) with cash on hand (Q3 10-Q page:3, page:10; Q3 release page:3). The effect is a simpler, fully unsecured debt stack with lower interest cost, but one in which several subsidiary guarantees were also released (Q3 10-Q page:10). No sponsor is identified, no controlling holder is disclosed and no dividend recapitalisation is documented in the supplied sources. Distributions resumed with a dividend declared in December 2025 and a 2.5 billion buyback authorized in March 2026, funded in the nine months from operating cash flow rather than new debt (10-K page:62; Q1 release page:4; Q3 10-Q page:3, page:28). Behaviour read at issuer level: Supportive on deleveraging and reporting transparency, Neutral or Mixed on capital allocation because debt is being repaid while distributions rise, and unresolved on the release of security and guarantees because the documents that permit and govern it are not supplied.

### Transaction summary and new debt issues

Unification and redomiciliation (status: completed May 2026). The boards of Carnival Corporation and Carnival plc recommended unifying the dual listed company under Carnival Corporation as the single listed parent, with Carnival plc shareholders receiving shares on a one-for-one basis and a move of incorporation from Panama to Bermuda; the plan was described as expected to preserve shareholder voting and economic rights (10-K page:7, management language). It was subject to shareholder, regulatory and UK court approvals and shareholder meetings in April 2026 (10-K page:8). The Q2 10-Q states it was completed in May 2026 (Q2 10-Q page:5) and the exhibit list of the Q3 10-Q includes a termination agreement dated May 6, 2026 between the corporation and Carnival plc and the memorandum and bye-laws of Carnival Corporation Ltd. (Q3 10-Q page:28). Uses of proceeds and debt raised: none, it is a share exchange with related costs shown in equity (Q3 10-Q page:4). Liquidity effect: not stated in the sources. Creditor mechanics: debt that was previously issued or guaranteed by "substantially the same entities" remains so (Q3 10-Q page:10), the obligor perimeter for a planned shelf is Carnival Corporation Ltd. with Carnival UK Ltd. (Q3 10-Q page:26), and the treatment of the former Carnival plc debt guarantees is not described. The sources do not give debt-document terms, so legal capacity for any future priming or release is Insufficient Information.

New debt issues, fiscal 2025 (status: completed). Senior unsecured notes: 1.3 billion 5.13% due 2029, 1.0 billion 5.75% due 2030, 1.0 billion 5.88% due 2031, 1.2 billion 4.13% euro notes due 2031, 3.0 billion 5.75% due 2032 and 2.0 billion 6.13% due 2033; unsecured term loans maturing in 2027 of 0.4 billion, 0.3 billion and 0.3 billion at SOFR plus 1.13%, 1.25% and 1.38%; a 4.5 billion unsecured multi-currency revolving credit facility maturing June 2030 with a 1.0 billion accordion; 0.8 billion of export credit borrowings (10-K page:80, page:81). Use of proceeds: with cash on hand, they prepaid 7.63% notes due 2026, 5.75% notes due 2027, first-priority secured term loans due 2027 and 2028, 10.38% senior priority notes due 2028, 6.00% notes due 2029 and 10.50% notes due 2030, an aggregate 11.6 billion, with 409 of debt extinguishment and modification costs including 271 premium paid (10-K page:81). Liquidity effect: 6.4 billion of liquidity at November 30, 2025 with 4.5 billion revolver availability (10-K page:59). Maturity effect: the new notes mature in 2029 to 2033 (10-K page:79).

Fiscal 2026 to August 31, 2026 (status: completed unless stated). No new debt issued (Q3 10-Q page:3). The 1.1 billion 5.75% convertible notes were settled in December 2025: 69.1 million shares issued and 500 cash (Q3 10-Q page:10). The 7.00% notes due 2029 (500) became unsecured in June 2026 and were then redeemed with cash on hand, with 23 of extinguishment costs (Q3 10-Q page:10; Q3 release page:3). The 7.88% notes due 2027 and 4.00% notes due 2028 are no longer secured, and the company states it has no remaining secured debt (Q3 10-Q page:10; Q3 release page:3, management language). Several unsecured notes, loans and export credit facilities are no longer subject to subsidiary guarantees (Q3 10-Q page:10). Rating events: a Moody's upgrade with a positive outlook (Q2 release page:3) and an S&P upgrade giving a second investment grade rating (Q3 release page:3); levels are not supplied. Planned: a Form S-3 expected on September 29, 2026 for debt securities guaranteed by Carnival UK Ltd. (Q3 10-Q page:26, status: expected, not confirmed as filed). Total debt moved from 27,383 to 24,559 and liquidity from 6,428 to 5,720 (CP-1). Shareholder-return actions: dividend reinstated in December 2025 at 0.15 per share quarterly; initial 2.5 billion buyback announced in March 2026 without expiry; dividends of 618 and repurchases of 929 in the nine months (10-K page:62; Q1 release page:4; Q3 10-Q page:3).
### Ownership and control

- Ownership. No controlling holder, sponsor or ownership percentage is disclosed in the supplied sources (Insufficient Information). The company is publicly listed; the number of record holders and shares outstanding are in the profile above.

- Control rights. Before May 2026 the two companies were run as one economic enterprise with identical boards and a single executive team (10-K page:7). After the unification there is one listed parent whose subsidiary Carnival UK Ltd. is wholly owned (Q3 10-Q page:26).

- Prior ownership and dividend recapitalisation history. Not covered by the supplied sources, which span fiscal 2025 and 2026; the 10-K states only that the dividend was reinstated in December 2025 (10-K page:62) (Insufficient Information for any earlier period).

- Minority interests. Noncontrolling interests of 19 at August 31, 2026, associated with subsidiaries that operate Isla Tropicale and Amber Cove (Q3 10-Q page:3, page:5); equity-method interests include 33 percent of Grand Bahama Shipyard and of Floating Docks and 45 percent of White Pass at November 30, 2025 (10-K page:78, page:79).

### Credit translations

- Revenue durability. Evidence: advance bookings and customer deposits of 7,639 (Q3 release page:9) with record 2027 booked occupancy and pricing stated by management (Q3 release page:1). Mechanic: deposits and balance payments arrive before voyage cost, so cash converts early and revenue is visible several months ahead; most revenue is ticket (65.0 percent) and sourced largely from United States guests (55.8 percent of nine-month revenue, Q3 10-Q page:8). Implication: revenue is durable in ordinary conditions, but a sourcing-market or geopolitical shock lands on a concentrated base and on a peak quarter that earns 60.4 percent of nine-month operating income; the Q2 release cites disruption in the Mediterranean from the Middle East conflict (Q2 release page:2). Countering conflict: none logged.

- Margin and cash-flow risk. Evidence: fuel 615 against 451 in the quarter and operating income down despite revenue growth (Q3 10-Q page:2). | CP-1A | e6bdf4e8a0bd7f9bc2074387f01e5f1005e099ab84dc85660b5d32b8e2059665 | Business model, structural change, capital allocation behaviour, conflicts. Its readiness judgment of this module is "Ready with limitations". |
Locators in brackets name the handoff and its section, for example [CP-1, Chart data: leverage]. Source locators are in those handoffs.
## Findings
### Reader summary
| Bottom line | Confidence | Main limitation |

| Credit view is strong and improving but not yet earnings-led: net debt to EBITDA fell to 3.19x through debt repayment, with liquidity of USD 5,720 million, while EBITDA was flat and cash returns to shareholders are rising. | Medium | Indentures, covenant ratios, rating levels and fiscal 2025 adjusted EBITDA are not supplied, so legal ranking and covenant headroom cannot be assessed. |
| Finding | Creditor impact | Confidence |

| Debt fell to USD 24,559 million and net debt to EBITDA to 3.19x, but EBITDA barely moved. | Leverage gains depend on continued repayment or on earnings growth, which has not yet appeared. | Medium |

| Liquidity of USD 5,720 million covers current debt of USD 2,036 million, but scheduled principal through 2030 is USD 13,295 million. | Refinancing access matters from 2027; rating levels that support it are not supplied. | Medium |
| Demand visibility is high but peaks in the third quarter and in United States guests, and loss of earnings is uninsured. | A shock falls on cash flow with no insurance offset. | High |
| Distributions and USD 18.3 billion of ship commitments compete with deleveraging. | Management discretion decides how fast leverage falls. | Medium |
| Legal ranking, covenant headroom and rating levels cannot be assessed from the pack. | Structural conclusions are provisional. | High |
### Credit view

Carnival Corporation Ltd. has a strong and improving fundamental credit profile, but its improvement so far comes from repaying debt rather than from earnings growth. Its strongest support is visible, deposit-funded demand (customer deposits of USD 7,639 million) and liquidity of USD 5,720 million with debt that is now unsecured and falling, to USD 24,559 million at August 31, 2026. The weakest point is that LTM EBITDA of USD 7,311 million is almost unchanged from USD 7,273 million for fiscal 2025, while fuel costs rise, loss of earnings is uninsured, and shareholder returns and USD 18.3 billion of ship commitments compete for cash. What decides the outcome is whether EBITDA grows enough to keep net debt to EBITDA, now 3.19x, falling while distributions rise.
### Credit assessment
| Element | Content | Category | Confidence | Basis |

| Assessment | Strong, improving fundamental credit profile with leverage of 3.36x total debt to EBITDA and 3.19x net debt to EBITDA on unadjusted EBITDA, liquidity of USD 5,720 million and no secured debt; the improvement is debt-led and the legal position of creditors is not assessable | Analyst Interpretation | Medium | CP-1 leverage and liquidity charts; CP-1A business and transaction view, governance table |

| Thesis | Carnival's visible, deposit-funded demand supports a falling debt balance, but creditors rely on EBITDA growth and on management's choice between debt reduction, shareholder returns and ship spending to keep leverage falling | Analyst Interpretation | Medium | CP-1 financial base view; CP-1A capital allocation table |

| Confidence limit | Confidence is below High because CP-1A rates this module "Ready with limitations" and because ranking, covenants, ratings and fiscal 2025 adjusted EBITDA are not supplied | Documentary Fact | Not applicable | CP-1A consumers table; CP-0 gaps |
### Key findings

First, leverage fell because debt fell, not because earnings grew. Total debt (principal) fell from USD 27,383 million at November 30, 2025 to USD 24,559 million at August 31, 2026, while LTM EBITDA (operating income plus depreciation and amortization, unadjusted) rose only from USD 7,273 million to USD 7,311 million; total debt to EBITDA moved from 3.77x to 3.36x and net debt to EBITDA from 3.50x to 3.19x [CP-1, Chart data: leverage]. Because the repayment was funded from cash, net debt rose by USD 12 million over the third quarter, from USD 23,327 million to USD 23,339 million, while the company paid dividends of USD 204 million and repurchased shares worth USD 549 million in the quarter [CP-1, Financial base view]. For creditors this means the next step down in leverage requires either further repayment, which competes with distributions, or EBITDA growth.

Second, near-term liquidity is sound but maturities depend on refinancing or cash flow. Liquidity is USD 5,720 million (cash USD 1,220 million plus USD 4,500 million available under a revolving facility maturing in June 2030) against current debt of USD 2,036 million, and no letters of credit usage is printed [CP-1, Chart data: liquidity]. Scheduled principal is USD 301 million for the remainder of 2026, USD 2,517 million in 2027, USD 3,961 million in 2028, USD 3,631 million in 2029 and USD 2,885 million in 2030 [CP-1, Chart data: debt maturities], which total USD 13,295 million through 2030 against LTM cash from operations less capital expenditure of USD 3,176 million. Management states the company has two investment grade ratings, and the revolver pricing is linked to ratings, but rating levels are not supplied [CP-1A, Transaction summary and new debt issues]. The implication is that debt service is comfortable but principal reduction at the recent pace relies on cash flow, and a larger part relies on market access.

Third, operating earnings are flat while costs rise, which limits cushion. In the third quarter revenue was USD 8,435 million against USD 8,153 million, while operating income was USD 2,220 million against USD 2,271 million, as fuel expense rose to USD 615 million from USD 451 million [CP-1, Financial base view]. Net income benefited from lower interest (USD 285 million in the quarter against USD 317 million) and lower debt extinguishment costs. Accrual EBITDA to interest expense is 6.21x on an LTM basis, but cash interest cover exists only for fiscal 2025 at 6.06x [CP-1, Chart data: interest cover]. Management guides fiscal 2026 adjusted EBITDA to approximately USD 7.14 billion, a management forecast rather than a result [CP-1, Latest quarter and after]. Fuel exposure is therefore the main near-term earnings swing factor for debt service.

Fourth, the business model gives revenue visibility but concentrates risk in time and place. Revenue is 65.0 percent ticket and 35.0 percent onboard, 55.8 percent of nine-month revenue comes from United States guests, and the third quarter produces 60.4 percent of nine-month operating income; customer deposits fund operations and form part of a working capital deficit of USD 9.1 billion [CP-1A, Company and operating model]. The company states it carries no insurance for loss of earnings or revenue [CP-1A, Company and operating model]. A disruption in the peak quarter or in United States demand would reach cash flow directly, and deposits that include refundable amounts (no split is given) could be called.

Fifth, the debt structure became simpler, with less structural protection for some holders (an interpretation). After the May 2026 unification into one Bermuda parent, all debt is unsecured, the 7.00% notes were redeemed, and notes, loans and export credit facilities of about USD 12,520 million on the recast basis moved to the no-subsidiary-guarantee category [CP-1, Debt schedule; CP-1A, Transaction summary and new debt issues]. The obligor group planned for a guaranteed shelf earned 45.3 percent of consolidated nine-month revenue [CP-1, Perimeter and reporting basis]. The cause of the releases, indenture terms and guarantor lists are not supplied, so ranking by legal entity is not assessable and conclusions about structure are provisional.

Sixth, capital allocation is the main discretionary variable. Dividends of USD 618 million and repurchases of USD 929 million in nine months equal 48.9 percent of cash from operations less capital expenditure; management targets distributing more than 40 percent of cash from operations by 2029 and a net debt to adjusted EBITDA ratio of 2.75x, and ship commitments have risen to USD 18.3 billion against USD 10.7 billion of undrawn export credit [CP-1, Cash flow and capital returns; CP-1A, Capital allocation and governance behaviour]. For comparison, reaching 2.75x on the unadjusted metric used here would need net debt lower by USD 3,234 million at constant EBITDA, or EBITDA of USD 8,487 million at constant net debt (see Calculations); the management target is defined on adjusted EBITDA and a minimum cash balance, so this is an illustration of scale only. Creditors depend on management choosing deleveraging over faster distributions, and the documents that could constrain that choice are not supplied.
### Strengths and weaknesses

Strengths. The business has high demand visibility: customer deposits of USD 7,639 million, record 2027 booked occupancy and pricing as stated by management, and 93 percent of 2026 booked at the time of the second quarter release [CP-1A, Company and operating model], so revenue and cash arrive ahead of voyage cost. The group is diversified across eight brands and two segments, with 94 ships and 272,380 lower-berth capacity, so a problem at one brand does not stop the group [CP-1A, Company profile]. Debt is falling, now unsecured, and mostly fixed-rate (52 percent fixed plus 33 percent euro fixed), with euro debt (43 percent including floating) matched against euro-functional operations, which limits rate and currency sensitivity [CP-1, Debt schedule]. Liquidity of USD 5,720 million exceeds current debt of USD 2,036 million, and USD 10.7 billion of undrawn export credit pre-funds part of the ship commitments [CP-1, Liquidity].

Weaknesses. EBITDA growth has stalled at the operating line while fuel and other costs rise, so leverage improvement relies on repayment [CP-1, Financial base view]. Loss of earnings is uninsured and the peak quarter and United States guests concentrate exposure [CP-1A, Company and operating model]. Ship commitments of USD 18.3 billion, of which USD 11.4 billion falls after 2030, and rising shareholder returns place long-dated claims on cash flow [CP-1, Claims outside the debt figure]. Creditor protection is less certain than the ratings story suggests, because security and several guarantees were released and the governing documents, covenant ratios and rating levels are not supplied [CP-1A, Monitoring items the source set lacks]. The headline leverage measure used by the company changed definition between releases, and fiscal 2025 adjusted EBITDA is missing, so the company's own leverage cannot be rebuilt [CP-1A, Conflicts logged].
### Key credit risks
| Risk | Mechanic | Credit implication | Severity |

| Fuel and cost inflation | Fuel expense rose to USD 615 million from USD 451 million in the quarter and operating income fell; a 10 percent move in fuel cost per ton moves fourth quarter adjusted net income by USD 59 million (management figure) | Reduces EBITDA growth that deleveraging depends on | Material |

| Distributions outpace deleveraging | Shareholder returns of USD 1,547 million in nine months and a stated target to distribute more than 40 percent of cash from operations by 2029; net debt flat in the third quarter | Leverage tolerance depends on a management choice | Material |

| Refinancing of 2027 to 2030 maturities | USD 12,994 million due in 2027 to 2030 against LTM cash from operations less capital expenditure of USD 3,176 million | Requires market access; rating levels not supplied | Material |

| Uninsured disruption in the peak quarter | No loss-of-earnings insurance; 60.4 percent of nine-month operating income in the third quarter; deposits partly refundable | Cash flow and liquidity shock without offset | Material |

| Structural and legal uncertainty | Security and guarantee releases; obligor group earns 45.3 percent of revenue; documents not supplied | Ranking and recovery mechanics cannot be assessed | Material |
| Covenant measurability | Compliance is stated but ratios are not printed; book proxies differ from definitions | Headroom unknown, though liquidity and equity are large | Minor |
| Interest rate and currency | 85 percent of debt is fixed; 43 percent is euro debt matched to euro operations | Limited near-term sensitivity | Minor |
## Calculations
